title: A Bell for the Harvest
premise: Jonah Galloway, a skeptical new teacher at Hollow Creek Elementary, arrives in a town where one student vanishes from every graduating class—and no one will say why. As the mirrors in her rented house begin lagging a second behind reality, she uncovers the town's founding bargain: each harvest, a child is 'invited in' to something beneath the school, and the adults' collective forgetting is the price of everyone else's survival. When the entity chooses her most vulnerable student, Milo, Jonah must decide whether to preserve her own safe detachment or trade her memories—and her sense of who she is—to take his place. She rings the schoolhouse's buried bell at sunrise, breaking the cycle at the cost of remembering nothing of the town, the children, or the person she briefly became.
about_author: Freya Sandoval is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent seven years in towns small enough that everyone remembered what you'd rather forget. She writes horror about the bargains communities make and the people who refuse to sign.

chapters.title: The Long Road In
chapters.summary: Jonah arrives in Hollow Creek at dusk, taking the cheap rental house no one else wanted. POV: Jonah. She notes the town's too-polite warmth and the absence of children playing outside. Emotional beat: uneasy optimism, the skeptic settling in.

chapters.title: Twenty-Six Faces
chapters.summary: First day teaching; Jonah counts twenty-six students but the attendance roster lists twenty-seven. POV: Jonah. The empty desk in the back row is dust-free. Emotional beat: professional curiosity shading into wrongness.

chapters.title: What the Principal Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Principal Voss deflects Jonah's questions with practiced ease; a custodian, Edie, warns her to 'count the chairs, not the children.' POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: first crack in her certainty that small towns are merely insular.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: At home, Jonah notices her mirror reflection lags—raising a hand a beat too late. She tests it with a stopwatch and a candle. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: the skeptic's thrill of an explainable phenomenon curdling into dread.

chapters.title: The Harvest Pageant
chapters.summary: Jonah attends the town's autumn festival, where children sing a counting song with one verse everyone skips. A parent's smile doesn't reach her eyes. POV: Jonah, with an interlude from Edie. Emotional beat: communal performance hiding communal fear.

chapters.title: Milo
chapters.summary: Jonah connects with Milo, a quiet boy who draws the schoolhouse with a bell that isn't there and says 'she rings it when it's time.' POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: protective instinct awakening; she stops being merely an observer.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: Jonah finds yearbooks in the school basement: every class photo, one child's face is smudged, always in the back row. The oldest photo shows the schoolhouse with its bell intact. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: horror of pattern recognition.

chapters.title: Reflections in Agreement
chapters.summary: The lag worsens—now the mirrors show the room as it was moments ago, and once, briefly, someone standing behind her who isn't there. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: isolation; she can no longer trust her own senses.

chapters.title: Edie's Confession
chapters.summary: Edie tells Jonah about the 'Invitation': the founders' bargain that feeds one child to what lives beneath the school so the rest prosper and forget. Edie's sister was invited in 1961; Edie alone remembers. POV: Edie, then Jonah. Emotional beat: grief and the burden of being the only one who remembers.

chapters.title: The Forgetting
chapters.summary: Jonah wakes unable to recall her sister's face; her phone photos of home are blank gray rectangles. The town's forgetting is contagious, and she's been breathing it for weeks. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: terror of identity erosion—the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: Twenty-Six Again
chapters.summary: A student, Cara, is absent. The class behaves as if she never existed; the roster reads twenty-six. Only Milo looks at the empty chair. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: guilt—she saw the pattern and did nothing fast enough.

chapters.title: Beneath the Schoolhouse
chapters.summary: Jonah and Milo find a bricked cellar door behind the boiler room, warm to the touch, humming like a struck bell. Something on the other side hums back when Milo speaks. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: dread of proximity; the entity is aware of them.

chapters.title: Voss's Bargain
chapters.summary: Principal Voss admits the truth: the town renews the Invitation each harvest because the alternative—the year the bell was silenced—killed the crops and half the town. He begs Jonah to leave before she's 'counted.' POV: Voss, then Jonah. Emotional beat: the banality of complicity; Voss is a father, not a monster.

chapters.title: The Choice of Names
chapters.summary: Jonah learns the entity chooses by invitation: someone must speak a child's name into the cellar. The town rotates the shame; this year it's Voss's turn, and his daughter is the same age as Milo. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: moral vertigo—there is no clean side.

chapters.title: What the Mirror Keeps
chapters.summary: The mirrors now show Jonah a life she doesn't remember: herself as a child in Hollow Creek, in the back-row desk. The lag isn't a delay—it's showing her what was taken. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: shattering revelation; her skepticism was itself a forgetting.

chapters.title: Run, Little Bell
chapters.summary: Milo is marked—the humming follows him home. Jonah tries to flee with him, but the town's roads loop back; the harvest boundary holds until dawn. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: desperate flight, claustrophobic futility.

chapters.title: The Invitation
chapters.summary: At midnight the town gathers at the school, faces slack with borrowed peace, Voss weeping as he opens the cellar. The entity speaks through every mirror in town at once, in Jonah's own childhood voice. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: climax of dread—the horror is communal and intimate.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Jonah realizes the lag was the entity's mistake—her reflection has been acting one second ahead, showing her the countermove before she makes it. She sees herself ringing the buried bell. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: reversal; her unbelief becomes strategy—she acts on faith in her own reflection.

chapters.title: The Bell Beneath
chapters.summary: Jonah breaks the brick, seizes the rope as the entity offers her everything she's forgotten—her sister, her childhood, her whole self—if she stops. She rings the bell through the entity's scream. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: climax; sacrifice of memory as the price of survival, inverted.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dawn. The mirrors reflect in real time. The cellar is cold stone and nothing else; the smudged children's faces in the yearbooks are clear and smiling, remembered at last. Cara and the others walk out of the mist at the town's edge. POV: multiple townsfolk, then Jonah. Emotional beat: exhausted, disbelieving relief.

chapters.title: The Price
chapters.summary: The town remembers everything now, and grieves together. Jonah, however, recalls nothing of Hollow Creek—only a warm feeling and a boy's drawing she keeps without knowing why. Milo visits her classroom and says thank you; she doesn't know for what. POV: Milo, then Jonah. Emotional beat: bittersweet cost; identity traded for others' wholeness.

chapters.title: A Bell for the Harvest
chapters.summary: Months later, Jonah finds a package: the small bell from the schoolhouse, and a note in Edie's hand—'Some things are worth not remembering.' In her window mirror, for one second, her reflection smiles before she does. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: quiet, open-ended grace—the past gently refusing to stay forgotten.
